target_customer: Young aspiring entrepreneurs worldwide who want to open a low cost mobile coffee cafe
problem: People without much money could not afford to open a cafe, shop or restaurant.
business_model: Sale of bicycle cafe carts and a brand franchise with monthly fee; buyers keep 90 percent of revenue
product_category: Franchise of bicycle mounted organic cafes

founders.name: Tomas Mazetti
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch July 2015 describes earlier activism projects; no career details.

founders.name: Maria De La Croix
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder and CEO in the 2016 FundedByMe press release; not in the YC founder list.

founders.name: Per Cromwell
founders.background_notes: Listed twice on the YC page; TechCrunch names him a co-founder.

exit.reason: No closure or sale notice found for the cafe business.

competitors.name: Starbucks
competitors.what: Global coffee chain that coverage framed Wheelys as taking on
competitors.traction_then: The founder cited about 28,000 Starbucks locations in America

technical_complexity.rationale: Designing and manufacturing a rugged bicycle cart with solar power and optional tablets is product design and supply chain work rather than research.

defensibility.rationale: Carts and coffee are easy to copy, and the open source style system leaned on brand rather than structural protection.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows incumbents responding. The company later moved toward unmanned mobile stores.

market_need_then: TechCrunch in July 2015 reported about 150 carts sold or pre-ordered in about 20 countries, with one or two sold per day, and a February 2015 post cited 50 cafes sold in nine months.

identity.logo: Identity created by the agency PJADAD per a design project page
identity.visual_style: Organic, solar and body powered bicycle cafe look
identity.voice_and_tone: Activist and anti-chain, positioned against fast food and Starbucks

branding.brand_signature: The bicycle cafe cart as an eco entrepreneur kit
branding.community_and_virality: Wide press (TechCrunch, Entrepreneur, NPR style food bike coverage, road.cc) and a record overfunded 2016 crowd campaign with 167 investors.

brand_strength.rationale: Strong press attention, a designed identity and an activist founder story drove coverage and a record crowd round, though sales stayed small.

pivots.to: Unstaffed mobile store (Moby Mart) piloted in Shanghai
pivots.why: Not stated in sources opened; press describes it as a new retail concept built with Hefei University of Technology.

outcome_analysis: Wheelys sold bicycle cafe carts to entrepreneurs in dozens of countries and gained heavy press and a record 2016 crowd round, then turned in 2017 to an unstaffed mobile store called Moby Mart. The directory marks the company inactive, but no source states a closure date or cause, so the cause is not public and failure factors stay empty.
notes: The company website returned a 503 so no site check was made. CB Insights reports 3.75 million dollars over five rounds with a latest 0.83 million round in Aug 2016 and ZoomInfo reports 3.3 million over two rounds, but these are single database figures with no round detail, so only the YC angels and the FundedByMe campaign (over 740,000 euros, about 410 percent of goal, so left null in dollars) are recorded. The Indiegogo campaign of July 2015 has no reported amount. The YC page says over 800 cafes in 75 countries while other pages say 250 cafes in 50 countries. The pivot to Moby Mart comes from search listings (TheNextWeb June 2017), not an opened page.
